When to reach for it

The (h+1)-th most-cited paper has more than h citations, i.e. at least h+1
If true, there are h+1 papers with ≥ h+1 citations
Stops at the end of the list; also short-circuits before indexing
Count how many leading papers satisfy the rule

p: `[3,0,6,1,5]` sorted descending is `[6, 5, 3, 1, 0]`:

blocks.h: Why does the first failure end the search?
p: After sorting, `citations[h]` can only go down while `h` goes up, so once `citations[h] > h` fails it fails for every larger h. The loop's final `h` is therefore the largest value for which the top `h` papers all have at least `h` citations.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) from sorting; the loop is O(n).
Space: O(1) extra (sort in place; the input is modified).

274.takeaway: Sort descending and count how many papers satisfy citations[i] > i; the first failure stops it for good.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: If the candidate knows `i`, the candidate cannot be the celebrity, so `i` takes over
One question eliminates one person either way
Verification test for each other person
A celebrity knows nobody, and everybody knows them

p: 3 people; `knows` matrix `[[1,1,0],[0,1,0],[1,1,1]]` (row = who asks). Everybody knows person 1 and 1 knows nobody else. Total questions asked: 6.

blocks.h: Why does the elimination pass work?
bullets: If `knows(cand, i)` is true, `cand` knows someone, so `cand` cannot be a celebrity.
If it is false, `i` is not known by `cand`, but a celebrity must be known by everyone, so `i` cannot be the celebrity and `cand` stays.
So after each question exactly one person is eliminated, and after n−1 questions one candidate is left. It is the only possible celebrity, not necessarily a real one.

p: Elimination only proves nobody else could be the celebrity. The candidate might still know someone earlier in the list or be unknown to somebody, so each other person gets two checks. Total questions are at most (n−1) + 2(n−1) = 3n−3.

bullets: Time: O(n) calls to `knows` (at most 3(n−1)).
Space: O(1).

277.takeaway: Eliminate by comparison: each knows(a, b) discards one of the two; then verify the lone survivor.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Next position where a non-zero must go
Boundary: everything before `slow` is the non-zero prefix in original order
Moves the non-zero forward; the zero it replaces goes behind `fast`

blocks.h: Why swap and not just copy?
p: Copying non-zeros forward and then filling zeros at the end also works but takes a second pass. The swap puts the displaced zero behind `fast` at the same moment, so one pass suffices. When `slow == fast` (no zeros yet) the swap exchanges an element with itself, which is harmless.

At any time `nums[:slow]` holds the non-zeros seen so far in original order, and `nums[slow:fast]` contains only zeros. Because every non-zero keeps its left-to-right order, the relative order is preserved.

bullets: Time: O(n) — one pass.
Space: O(1) — in place.

283.takeaway: Two pointers (write index and read index): swap each non-zero to the write index to compact non-zeros while pushing zeros back.

p: Grid `INF -1 0 INF / INF INF INF -1 / INF -1 INF -1 / 0 -1 INF INF`. The gates are [(0, 2), (3, 0)]. Each pop fills its unvisited empty neighbours (in the order they are explored):

p: Distance to the nearest gate is exactly the BFS level when all gates start together, so each cell is reached once, by its nearest gate first.

p: The rule must use the old state for every cell. The code builds `nxt` and copies it back, costing O(m·n) extra space. The O(1)-space follow-up encodes the transition inside each cell (for example 2 = was alive, becomes dead; 3 = was dead, becomes alive), then decodes in a second pass.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Tells whether you can leave the opponent a multiple of 4
True when n is not a multiple of 4
That is exactly when the first player wins

p: Brute force over all moves (win means the player to move can force a win) agrees with `n % 4 != 0` for every n:

bullets: With 4 stones, any move (1–3) leaves 3, 2 or 1, and the opponent takes them all and wins.
With n not a multiple of 4, remove `n % 4` stones: you leave a multiple of 4 for the opponent.
After any move by the opponent (1–3) you can restore a multiple of 4 by removing `4 − (their move)`. So the player facing a multiple of 4 always loses with perfect play.
Time: O(1).
Space: O(1).

292.takeaway: Nim variant with moves 1–3: positions that are multiples of 4 are losing; leave your opponent a multiple of 4.

`heapq` only has a min-heap; negating makes the smallest stored number the largest real number
Its top is the smallest of the upper half
Add x to the lower half
Every new number first goes through `lo`
Guarantees every number in `lo` ≤ every number in `hi`
Peek the middle values in O(1)
Median needs only the two heap tops

p: Stream `5, 15, 1, 3` (lists shown sorted, `lo` as real values):

blocks.h: Why push-pop-pop instead of comparing x with the tops?
p: Passing x through `lo` and then moving `lo`'s maximum to `hi` guarantees the ordering invariant (max(lo) ≤ min(hi)) without an `if`, even when x belongs on the other side. The last line fixes the sizes: if `hi` got bigger, its minimum moves back so `lo` is the larger half and holds the odd middle element.

blocks.h: Why two heaps and not a sorted list?

bullets: Time: addNum O(log n) (three heap operations); findMedian O(1).
Space: O(n).

295.takeaway: Two heaps around the median: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced in size.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: One scan with a balance counter
Open → +1, close → −1; never negative, and zero at the end
Set of all strings with the same number of removals
A set removes duplicate strings created by deleting equal neighbours
Every way to delete exactly one bracket
Slicing out character i; letters are never removed
BFS: stop at the first level containing a valid string
The first level that succeeds uses the fewest removals

p: `s = '()())()'`. Each level is every string reachable with that many removals:

The goal is the minimum number of removals, and we want all results with that minimum. Level k holds every string with k brackets removed, so the first level with any valid string is the minimum, and all valid strings in that level are the answer: ['(())()', '()()()']. We never go to level k+1, so no string with more removals is returned.

blocks.h: Why a set of strings per level?
p: Removing either of two equal adjacent characters gives the same string (`'(('`). Using a set avoids exploring duplicates and also deduplicates the final answer.

bullets: Time: O(2ⁿ · n) worst case: up to 2ⁿ distinct subsequences, each validated in O(n).
Space: O(2ⁿ) for the largest level.

301.takeaway: BFS by number of deletions: the first level that contains a valid string is minimal, and all valid strings there are the answer.

Cell + block above + block to the left − overlap

Rectangle sum from four prefix values
Subtract top and left strips; add back the corner subtracted twice

p: `[[3,0,1],[5,6,3],[1,2,0]]` gives prefix table (with border):

`p[3][3] − p[1][3] − p[3][1] + p[1][1]` = 21 − 4 − 9 + 3 = 11, the sum 6 + 3 + 2 + 0. The big rectangle `p[3][3]` includes the top strip (`p[1][3]`) and left strip (`p[3][1]`) which both include the corner `p[1][1]`, so the corner is added back.
With many queries on a matrix that never changes, paying O(m·n) once makes each query four lookups.

Space: O(m·n) for the prefix table.

304.takeaway: 2-D prefix sums with inclusion–exclusion: any rectangle sum is four table lookups.

The size of the range that `tree[i]` covers
Sum of the `i & -i` elements ending at position i (1-based)
Each cell stores a block sum of power-of-two length
Jump to the next cell whose range includes this position
Update every block containing the element: O(log n) cells
Strip the lowest bit, moving to the previous block

Update blocks by the difference, not the new value; needs the stored `nums`
Range sum from two prefix sums

p: `nums = [1,3,5]`. After building, `tree = [1, 4, 5]` (positions 1–3: `tree[1]=1`, `tree[2]=1+3`, `tree[3]=5`). `sumRange(0,2)` = `_prefix(3) − _prefix(0)` = tree[3] + tree[2] = 9. Then `update(1, 2)`: delta = 2 − 3 = −1, i = 2 → `tree[2] += −1`, then i = 4 > n, stop. Now `tree = [1, 3, 5]` and `sumRange(0,2)` = 8.

blocks.h: Why a Fenwick tree rather than a prefix-sum array?
p: When updates and queries are mixed, the Fenwick tree balances both at O(log n).

bullets: Time: Update and sumRange O(log n); the constructor makes n updates, so O(n log n).
Space: O(n) for `tree` and `nums`.

307.takeaway: Fenwick (binary indexed) tree: lowest-bit jumps give O(log n) point updates and prefix sums.

Index of the final occurrence of each letter

Kept in increasing order whenever possible, which makes it lexicographically smallest

Top is larger than the new letter AND appears again later

stack

pop b (later copies exist), then push

p: For example when `a` arrives, `c` and `b` are both larger and both occur later, so they leave and `a` goes first. At index 6 (`b`), `d` is larger than `b` but `d`'s last index is 4 < 6, so `d` is never popped (see the table: the stack becomes `acdb`).

If it fails

The letter never appears again; popping it would lose it from the answer entirely

blocks.h: Why skip letters already on the stack?
p: If `c` is already in the stack, the stack so far is already the best arrangement with that letter included; adding a later copy could only make the result larger. The earlier copy would have been popped only if a smaller letter later had made that profitable, which is the pop rule's job.

bullets: Time: O(n) — each letter is pushed and popped at most once.
Space: O(1) — at most 26 letters in `st` and `seen` (O(n) for the `last` dict if the alphabet is unbounded).

316.takeaway: Monotonic stack with last-occurrence check: pop a larger top only if it will reappear later.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Integer square root: floor(√n), exact for large ints
Count perfect squares ≤ n without float rounding errors

p: The formula checked against a simulation of every round:

bullets: Bulb k is toggled once for each divisor of k (once in the round of each divisor).
Divisors usually come in pairs (d, k/d), so most bulbs are toggled an even number of times and end up off.
Only when k is a perfect square does one divisor pair with itself, giving an odd count, so exactly those bulbs end on.
The number of perfect squares in 1..n is ⌊√n⌋, which is `isqrt(n)`. For n = 3 that is 1 (just bulb 1).

p: Floating-point square roots can round wrongly for very large n (for example just below a perfect square), giving an off-by-one. `math.isqrt` works on integers exactly.

bullets: Time: O(1) for typical sizes (integer square root is cheap).
Space: O(1).

319.takeaway: Count perfect squares: a bulb ends on only if it has an odd number of divisors, so the answer is floor(sqrt(n)).

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: `dp[a]` = fewest coins for amount a; 0 coins for amount 0; infinity = unreachable so far
Min-DP needs an 'impossible' value that loses every `min`
`for c in coins: if c <= a`
Try each coin as the last coin used
Skip coins larger than the amount
Best for the remainder plus this coin
`inf + 1` stays `inf`, so unreachable amounts propagate safely
Keep the best over all coins

p: `coins = [1,2,5]`, `amount = 11`. Table of `dp[a]`:

Taking the largest coin first is not always optimal. With `coins = [1,3,4]` and `amount = 6`, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 uses only 2. The DP tries every coin as the last one for every amount, so it never commits to a bad first choice.

blocks.h: Why does unbounded supply fit this loop order?
p: `dp[a - c]` may already use coin c, so the same coin type can be reused any number of times. (For a 0/1 knapsack the iteration direction would be changed to prevent that.)

bullets: Time: O(amount · len(coins)).
Space: O(amount).

322.takeaway: Unbounded-knapsack min DP: dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a − coin]; infinity marks unreachable amounts.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Prefix sum → earliest index where it occurred; sum 0 occurs 'before index 0'
Lets subarrays starting at index 0 be found
Then the elements after that index sum to exactly k
Earliest start gives the longest subarray
Store the index only if the sum is new
Keeps the earliest index; later equal sums don't overwrite it

blocks.h: Why store only the first index?
p: For a fixed right end `i`, a smaller start index means a longer subarray, so only the earliest index of each prefix sum matters. `setdefault` leaves the earliest in place (a plain `first[s] = i` would overwrite it and shorten answers). This also handles negative numbers, which is why a sliding window won't work here.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the map.

325.takeaway: Prefix sums plus a first-seen map: subarray (j, i] sums to k when prefix[i] − k appeared at j; the earliest j gives the longest.

What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Tail of the odd chain, tail of the even chain, and the head of the even chain
The even chain's head must be remembered to reattach it
Continue while an odd node follows `even`
`even` may be None (even-length input) or the last node
Link the next odd node and advance
Skips over the even node between them
Link the next even node and advance
Same for the even chain, using the updated `odd`
Attach the even chain after the odd chain
Final stitch; the last even node's `next` is already None

blocks.h: Why two separate pointers advancing together?
p: Each pass of the loop moves one node from the original sequence into each chain, so the relative order within each chain is preserved. No nodes are created or copied; only `next` pointers change, which keeps the space at O(1).

`even` can be None right at the start (single node) or after a pass (even length), and `even.next` can be None (odd length, `even` at the last node). Both cases end the loop with `odd` at the last odd node, so `odd.next = evenHead` completes the list.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

328.takeaway: Two interleaved pointer chains: peel odd and even nodes into separate lists in place, then link the even list after the odd one.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Best possible start of an increasing pair
Smallest value that has a smaller value before it
Best possible middle of a triplet
`<=` so equal values replace, not extend
`n` is bigger than a `second` that has something smaller before it
Found i < j < k with increasing values

blocks.h: A subtle point: `first` can move after `second` is set
p: At the number 0, `first` becomes 0 while `second` is still 5. That looks like `first` is no longer before `second`, but it doesn't matter: `second = 5` still records that some earlier number (2 or 1) was smaller. Any later `n > 5` completes a real triplet using that earlier number. The invariant is 'there is a pair ending at `second`' and `first` only tries to improve future pairs.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

334.takeaway: Greedy two thresholds: keep the smallest start and the smallest middle seen; any number above the middle completes an increasing triplet.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Letter → how many times it is inside the window
`len(cnt)` is the number of distinct letters
Window has too many distinct letters
Shrink from the left until valid
Keeps `len(cnt)` equal to the distinct count

blocks.h: Why `while` and why delete zero counts?
p: One new letter can push `len(cnt)` above k, but dropping a single left letter may not reduce the distinct count (it might still appear later in the window), so the loop continues until a letter's count reaches 0. Deleting the zero entry is what makes `len(cnt)` fall; otherwise the loop would never terminate.

bullets: Time: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the window once.
Space: O(k) for the counter (at most k+1 entries).

340.takeaway: Sliding window with a counter: grow right, and while distinct letters exceed k shrink left, deleting zero counts.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The rule 'at least two parts' makes tiny n lose: breaking is worse than keeping, so special-case
Peel off 3s while more than 4 remains
3 is the best factor size to maximise a product for a given sum
Leftover 4 stays as 4 (2 × 2 = 4, no gain from splitting)

p: `n = 10`: loop: res = 3, n = 7; res = 9, n = 4; stop (n is not > 4). Result 9 × 4 = 36 (3 × 3 × 4). Checked against exhaustive search:

bullets: Splitting a part ≥ 5 into 2 and (part − 2) is better: 2·(part−2) > part when part > 4. So no part should be 5 or more.
A 4 can be left as 4 or split into 2 + 2, which give the same product, so 4 is allowed.
Prefer 3s over 2s: 3·3 = 9 beats 2·2·2 = 8 for the same sum 6, so use 2s only for the remainder.
Time: O(n) as written (n/3 iterations); O(log n) with exponentiation.
Space: O(1).

343.takeaway: Maximise a product with a fixed sum: use as many 3s as possible, leave 2 or 4 at the end, and special-case n ≤ 3.
